Class TimeStampMpscQueue

java.lang.Object
io.perl.api.impl.TimeStampMpscQueue
All Implemented Interfaces:
Queue<TimeStampNode>
public final class TimeStampMpscQueue extends Object implements Queue<TimeStampNode>
Lock-free intrusive multiple-producer, single-consumer timestamp queue.

Allocation model

Producers supply a single-use TimeStampNode; enqueue does not allocate. The node contains both the immutable timestamp payload and the linked-queue next reference. This removes the second allocation made by ConcurrentLinkedQueue for its private wrapper node.

Concurrency and memory ordering

Any number of producers may call add(TimeStampNode). Exactly one consumer owns poll() and clear(). Producers locate a trailing node and publish with a compare-and-set from a null successor to the new node. That successful compare-and-set is the enqueue linearization point. The consumer reads next with acquire semantics, which observes the immutable timestamp fields initialized before producer publication. Per-producer FIFO order and the global order of successful link operations are preserved.

The consumer owns the head and therefore advances it without a compare-and-set or an item-field compare-and-set. A lagging producer tail is only a traversal hint; failure to update it cannot lose an element. Under contention, a failed producer compare-and-set means another producer made progress, so the enqueue algorithm is lock-free.

Garbage collection

Consumed predecessor chains are detached in batches of 16. The consumer release-publishes a recovery head before self-linking every retired predecessor in the completed batch. A producer suspended with any stale pointer detects that self-link and resumes from the recovery head. Unlike JDK ConcurrentLinkedQueue, an intrusive node cannot null a separate item reference while retaining its structural wrapper. Self-linking removes each retired timestamp from the live queue chain and enables its payload and node to be reclaimed after stale producer, tail-hint, consumer, and caller references have also disappeared. It cannot make an object collectible while any such strong reference remains. Nodes are deliberately not pooled: pooling would retain heap, complicate ownership, and introduce ABA risks.

Like JDK ConcurrentLinkedQueue, the producer tail is allowed to lag by one node. Updating the shared tail only after a producer has traversed away from its initial tail candidate avoids a tail compare-and-set on every enqueue while preserving the linked-node compare-and-set as the linearization point.

Producer and consumer state live in separate, manually padded holder objects to reduce false sharing. This is a best-effort layout optimization: the Java language and HotSpot do not guarantee field order or cache-line placement. The implementation deliberately avoids the internal @Contended annotation because using it would require internal-module access and JVM flags in every embedding application. Padding is not part of the correctness argument.

Usage constraints

  • Only one thread may invoke poll or clear.
  • Each node may be enqueued exactly once.
  • The queue is unbounded; callers provide overload control.
